svg.text: WHY NOT JUST MAGNETS?
"Amazon has magnets that can handle that weight fine, and are cheap — why can't we just use those?"
A fair question, and the answer is arithmetic, not opinion. It takes three steps: what a rating measures, what the fridge actually does to it, and what a lever does to whatever is left.
PULL — what the box quotes
tension
Straight away from the surface. Ratings are measured
THIS way, on thick ground steel at zero gap. Strongest
direction by far.
SHEAR — what gravity applies
gravity
Sliding DOWN the panel. The magnet only resists through
friction: grip = pull x mu, and mu is tiny on smooth
paint. Weakest direction.
PEEL — what a bump applies
pry
Levering one edge away. The prying force is multiplied
by the lever, and it lands on ONE magnet at a time —
never on the total.
WATCH THE NUMBER ON THE BOX COLLAPSE
The as-built magnet is a 48 mm (1.89 in) pot magnet, and its catalogue rating is honest — for the test it describes. The fridge is not that test.
RATED 175 lbf (778 N)
measured on THICK ground steel, ZERO gap, pulling STRAIGHT OFF
x 0.35 on the fridge = 61.2 lbf (272 N) PULL
0.6-0.9 mm painted sheet: thin steel saturates, paint holds the magnet off the metal
x mu 0.2 friction = 12.2 lbf (54 N) SHEAR
the load is SLIDING, not pulling — bare nickel on smooth paint barely grips
12.2 lbf (54 N) is 7% of the number on the box — in the direction the fridge actually loads it.
Not our theory — the vendors publish the drop themselves.
totalElement rate their 43 mm rubber pot magnet at 33.5 lbf (149 N) vertical pull but only 7.0 lbf (31 N) horizontal — 21% of the headline, from their own catalogue.
PEEL: YOU NEVER FIGHT THE TOTAL
Four magnets at 61 lbf (272 N) each sounds like 245 lbf
(1090 N) of holding. It is not. Bump the screen's top edge
and the plate rotates about its bottom — the prying force is
multiplied by the lever ratio, and the whole moment lands on
the TOP magnet alone, at its own 61 lbf. The instant it lets
go, its share dumps onto the next one down. Magnet mounts do
not fail by being overpowered; they fail by unzipping, one
magnet at a time.
small pry,
long lever
pivot
fails first
WHAT MAGNET-ONLY WOULD ACTUALLY NEED
Hanging load: display 8.7 lbf (39 N) + bracket 12.8 lbf (57 N)
Rated pull needed per pound held, in shear: 1 / (0.35 x 0.2)
= 14 lbf rated per lbf held
So holding 21.5 lbf (96 N) in shear needs
~307 lbf (1.4 kN) RATED — 14x whatever it holds, before any
safety factor
And if the panel is 304 stainless (many are), every magnet contributes
exactly ZERO. This one measured magnetic — the design still must not care.
THE ANSWER: DON'T FIGHT THE PHYSICS — HOOK OVER THE TOP
fridge
all 21.5 lbf (96 N) of it
bearing: the fridge TOP carries the weight
magnets
The arm rests ON the fridge top. The vertical load goes into bearing at the corner — compression on painted
steel over a sponge pad.
The magnets carry ZERO vertical load. They only stop swing and rattle, and that duty is TENSION — their
strong direction.
Demand on a magnet: 1.6 lbf (7 N) from a firm 5 lbf (22 N) touch press, 2.1 lbf (9 N) of total peel —
against 61 lbf (272 N) of derated capacity each: 37x in hand.
A non-magnetic panel no longer matters: the hook still carries everything, and the arm's width still resists
the twist.
The stakes: 3.94 kg (8.7 lb) of optically bonded glass over a kitchen floor. "Probably strong enough" is not
a spec — a hook is.
SO HOW STRONG WOULD THEY HAVE TO BE? — the fair answer
To hold 21.5 lbf (96 N) by friction alone, TOTAL rated pull across all magnets (divide by 0.070):
SF 1.0
on the edge of sliding
= 38 lbf x 8 magnets
SF 2.5
project standard
= 96 lbf x 8 magnets
SF 4.0
overhead glass
= 154 lbf x 8 magnets
The magnets already specified are 175 lbf each. Eight of them give 98.0 lbf (436 N) of shear — SF 4.6.
So shear is NOT the reason for the hook. Magnets can carry this weight. The hook is there for what shear numbers do not cover:
PEEL — a lever at one corner beats a single magnet, not the total, and the rest unzip after it.
A NON-MAGNETIC panel makes every one of those numbers zero. This one measured magnetic; the design still must not
depend on it.
CREEP — magnets under sustained shear on painted steel slide slowly. An SF that holds today need not hold in a year.
The failure mode is bonded glass onto a kitchen floor, with no warning.
